description: Hey! I’m a Swiss CS student focused on backend algorithms (Java/Python). I’m tackling the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser, building the backend to crunch NASA’s 3D topography and orbital data for landing windows. I have the data pipeline covered, but need teammates for frontend (React/Vue), 3D visualization (Three.js), and UI/UX.
summary: Lunar Heuristics is a working web application that compares sunlight and Earth visibility at lunar locations using real NASA/JPL Horizons data. Users choose coordinates and dates, explore Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon and compare continuous periods when both are visible. A shared timeline, clearance sensitivity control and downloadable results make the trade-offs easy to inspect. For example, our bundled 30-day comparison shows that more total sunlight does not necessarily produce a longer continuous joint visibility window. The prototype supports education and early mission-planning discussion while clearly distinguishing geometric visibility from measured terrain, electrical power and communication-link feasibility.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Heuristics helps users compare lunar locations and dates through a single browser interface. It displays Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation, a time slider, visibility percentages, continuous joint visibility windows and estimated time to set within the analysis interval. Users can enter custom coordinates, compare three illustrative reference sites, adjust a uniform clearance threshold and export CSV data and provenance.

HOW IT WORKS

The application queries NASA/JPL Horizons for airless apparent Sun (10) and Earth (399) positions from a lunar observer (coord@301), at zero altitude above the reference surface. It uses hourly samples and linearly interpolates threshold crossings. It intersects Sun and Earth visibility intervals to identify simultaneous opportunities. Percentages are duration-weighted rather than counts of visible sample points. Each result retains the query parameters and raw JPL response. Three bundled datasets provide 721 hourly samples per reference site for 15 November–15 December 2026 UTC; other scenarios use the live API.

RESULTS AND VALUE

For the bundled 30-day period at zero-degree clearance, Polar site A (89.5 degrees south, 0 degrees east) has 100.0% Sun visibility and a longest joint window of 310.9 hours. Polar site B (85 degrees south, 30 degrees east) has 59.9% Sun visibility but a longer joint window of 378.4 hours. The comparison makes a useful trade-off visible more total sunlight does not necessarily yield a longer continuous period with both Sun and Earth visible. The interface supports educators, the public and early mission-planning discussions.

IMPLEMENTATION

The frontend uses JavaScript ES modules, HTML, CSS and SVG. A JavaScript API on Vercel fetches live NASA data, a Python standard-library server supports local use. No NASA API key is needed. Source code: https://github.com/medeeam/lunar-heuristics

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

This is an exploratory prototype, not a flight-planning product. The horizon is geometric and clearance is a uniform sensitivity mask, not measured topography. No LOLA terrain, eclipses or disk/limb effects are modeled. Hourly samples may miss short events. Solar incidence is not electrical power, and Earth-center visibility is not a radio-link budget or ground-station guarantee. Proposed next steps are LOLA-derived directional horizons, finer sampling near crossings and independent SPICE validation. These are future work, not current capabilities.
